bull.b: Record IET orders, a 2.2x book-to-bill ratio, and $37.1 billion of RPO provide substantial multi-year revenue visibility. This backlog supports capacity planning, improves confidence in future utilization, and strengthens Baker Hughes’ position in gas and industrial infrastructure markets.

Expanding EBITDA margins alongside robust free cash flow indicates improving operating execution and meaningful cash-generation capacity. These gains can support investment, debt reduction, and customer-service capabilities, making the business more resilient across energy and industrial cycles.

Chart broadens Baker Hughes into thermal management and industrial technologies while adding targeted cost and commercial synergies. Greater exposure to industrial, infrastructure, and aftermarket activities could diversify earnings and support a more durable margin and cash-generation profile.

bear.b: The sharp increase in debt-to-equity reduces financial flexibility and makes Baker Hughes more sensitive to cyclical demand changes. Although management plans to deleverage, the higher balance-sheet burden can constrain capital allocation and increase pressure on cash flows during weaker periods.

A sharply negative TTM revenue-growth reading and broadly flat 2025 revenue raise questions about the consistency of top-line expansion. Uneven revenue conversion can make planning more difficult, limit operating leverage, and reduce the durability of recent profitability improvements.

Strong IET bookings do not translate quickly into reported revenue when long-cycle orders convert beyond 2027. This timing gap can defer the financial benefit of backlog growth, create execution demands over several years, and leave near-term results less responsive to order momentum.
